Ability Amore: dating built
around accessibility, not bolted onto it.

Most dating apps treat disability as an edit-your-bio afterthought, if they acknowledge it at all. Ability Amore puts it in the core onboarding, on equal footing with every other compatibility signal — one focused question at a time, before a user ever sees a card to swipe.

01
01The Brief

Swipe apps optimize for speed. This one doesn't — not at the start.

The category's default pattern is a fast funnel: photo, bio, go. That's great for volume, bad for signal — people end up swiping on strangers with almost nothing real to go on. This design deliberately slows the front door down: a dedicated, single-focus screen for each meaningful attribute — height, smoking, drinking, exercise, accessibility needs, personality — before a user ever sees a card to swipe.

△

Problem

Thin profiles produce thin matches. A long, single monolithic sign-up form gets abandoned; a photo-only profile gives almost no compatibility signal at all.

◇

Approach

Break profile-building into a sequence of small, single-question screens — each one easy to answer, easy to skip, and easy to edit later — rather than one long form or a bare-minimum sign-up.

02
02The Onboarding Flow

Seven stages before the first swipe.

Grouped by intent rather than screen count — the real flow spans well over a dozen individual screens, but reads as seven clear decisions a new user moves through.

03
03Design Rationale

One question per screen, on purpose.

The single-focus pattern isn't just about reducing form fatigue during sign-up — it's built to be reused for the life of the profile, not thrown away after onboarding.

Built once, reused for editing

Height, Smoke, Alcohol, Exercise, Hobbies, and Who I Am each exist twice in the file — once during onboarding, once again as a standalone Edit screen under Settings. Same layout, same interaction, so a returning user never has to relearn how to update one fact about themselves.

Skippable without penalty

Each lifestyle-signal screen is a self-contained step with its own "Next" — a user who doesn't want to answer one question can move past it without the rest of the profile stalling.

Inclusion as its own step

Disability isn't folded into a generic "About You" field — it gets a dedicated screen, the same weight as any lifestyle question, not an afterthought buried in a text box.

A consistent shell, every screen

Status bar, back arrow, serif headline, single primary action pinned near the top — the same shell repeats across all onboarding and edit screens, so the "cost" of adding one more question is just content, not a new layout to design.

Onboarding — Your Height
One of ~12 single-question onboarding screens — same shell, same pattern, reused later as an Edit screen
04
04Match & Chat

Once the profile is real, the loop is familiar.

After the onboarding investment, the core loop stays close to the category's proven shape — card swipe, mutual like, celebration, conversation — rather than reinventing what already works for matching itself.

Swipe cardsBoostSuper LikeMatch celebrationComments on photosAudio & video call

↻Swipe Card Deck

The Home screen surfaces one profile at a time with reject, super-like, like, and boost actions — distance and first-line bio visible without opening a full profile.

♥Matches Tabs

Likes, Super Likes, and Comments as separate tabs on the Matches screen — comment activity on a user's own photos surfaced as its own engagement channel, not just likes.

✓"It's a Match"

A dedicated celebration screen with both profile photos, and an immediate choice — send a message or go back to swiping — removing friction at the exact moment intent is highest.

☎Chat, Audio & Video

Chats list with unread badges and new-connection avatars up top, plus dedicated in-app audio and video call screens — conversation doesn't have to leave the product.

05
05Safety, Privacy & Control

Control lives in settings, not an afterthought.

A dating app's settings surface is where trust actually gets tested — this one gives it real estate: discovery controls, granular privacy, and a direct way to block someone, not buried three menus deep.

◎Discovery Preferences

Separate from Match Preferences set during onboarding — a dedicated settings screen for adjusting who can find you, independent of the original setup flow.

🔒Profile Privacy

Its own settings screen, distinct from Account & Security — visibility controls treated as a different concern from login credentials.

⊘Block Users

A direct, named settings screen for blocking — not folded into a generic "report" flow.

⚙Account & Security

Change Password kept as its own screen, separate from general account settings — credential changes get a focused flow, same philosophy as the onboarding screens.

06
06Design System

A warm, editorial visual voice.

Serif headlines against a clean sans body — softer and more editorial than the typical geometric-sans dating-app look. Values below are the project's own named Coolors palette and typefaces pulled directly from the generated design context, not eyeballed from screenshots.

Component consistency: pill buttons at 50px radius with a soft drop shadow, a 2.5px outlined variant for secondary actions, and the same status-bar / home-indicator chrome on every screen.
07
07Status

Where it stands today.

This is a complete Figma design system — every screen in the flow above exists and is fully specified. It hasn't moved to code yet, so the honest status is design-complete, not shipped.
